title: Twenty cultures, twenty plates
hook: Does a drug make bacteria resistant, or were the mutants already there? One test can tell.

knows: resistant cells can exist before a drug arrives (antibiotic-already-there)
doesNotKnow: how anyone could tell random mutations before the drug from the drug making cells resistant
that the two ideas predict different spreads of counts across identical cultures

misconception: Mutations happen when the cell needs them: the drug makes some cells resistant. Then identical cultures should give similar counts.
objective: The learner can explain that random mutations during growth give very uneven counts across identical cultures (many plates with none, a few jackpots from early mutations copied into every descendant), while resistance made by the drug gives similar counts, and that this difference is how the fluctuation test tells the two ideas apart.

claims.text: Under the random-while-growing rule, counts across 20 identical cultures are very uneven: in the seed-1 run 9 of 20 plates had none and one had 128 (all counts: 1, 32, 6, 0, 0, 0, 8, 0, 0, 128, 1, 3, 0, 2, 8, 1, 0, 0, 0, 16).
claims.source: Demo.tsx runGrowing(), mulberry32 seed 1 (the start seed, not chosen for its result; the brief's check gives the same 20 counts). Brief check over 10,000 seeded runs (seed 99): 95.9% had a largest plate at least 5 times the median. Later seeds vary: seed 2 gives 8 empty and a largest of 6 (the reveal then says there was no big jackpot).
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Re-ran from my own copies of mulberry32 and the Poisson sampler (scratch ld.mjs): seed 1 counts 1, 32, 6, 0, 0, 0, 8, 0, 0, 128, 1, 3, 0, 2, 8, 1, 0, 0, 0, 16; 9 empty, max 128. Seed 2: 8 empty, max 6, as the source says. Seed 1 is the useState start value, not tuned. Over 2,000 other seeds the reveal's jackpot branch (max >= 2 x drug max) fires 42% of the time; the reveal text covers both branches.

claims.text: When the drug makes the mutations, with the same average of about 10 per plate, every plate gets a similar count: in the seed-1 run 0 plates had none and counts ran from 5 to 15.
claims.source: Demo.tsx runDrug(), Poisson(10) per plate, mulberry32 seed 1; Poisson variance = mean (brief: median variance/mean 1.0 over 10,000 runs).
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Same re-run, drug rule: seed 1 counts 9, 7, 8, 12, 7, 15, 13, 10, 8, 12, 7, 10, 12, 5, 12, 10, 9, 8, 8, 11; 0 empty, 5 to 15. 'Same average of about 10': drug mean is 10 by construction (simulated 10.00); growing rule expectation is sum over g of (2^g / 2^20) x 2^(19-g) = 20 x 2^19 / 2^20 = 10 (minus a negligible correction), so the averages match in expectation even though the growing rule's typical plate is far lower.

claims.text: A mutation early in growth is copied into every descendant, so it makes a large clone (a jackpot): a mutation at division g of 20 ends as 2^(20 - g) resistant cells, so the seed-1 plate of 128 came from one mutation at division 13.
claims.source: Each resistant daughter doubles at every later division; 2^(20-13) = 128. Demo.tsx records the first mutation's division for the largest plate.
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Derivation and code: a mutant formed at 0-indexed round g doubles in the 19 - g later rounds, 2^(19-g) cells; the stage numbers divisions from 1 (topGen + 1), so division g' gives 2^(20-g'). Re-run: the seed-1 plate of 128 had exactly one mutation event, at division 13 (2^7 = 128), so 'one mutation at division 13, copied' is literal here.

claims.text: Luria and Delbrück found jackpots like these in 1943, with a virus instead of a drug: evidence that resistance mutations arise at random before the threat, not in answer to it.
claims.source: Luria S.E. and Delbrück M. (1943) Mutations of bacteria from virus sensitivity to virus resistance, Genetics 28: 491-511 (brief citation). Unverified: needs a human source check, including the citation details. If it fails, cut this sentence from the reveal; the lesson stands on c1-c3.
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): HELD. Luria and Delbrück (1943), Genetics 28: 491-511, could not be opened (journal, PubMed and library hosts blocked; only GitHub and PyPI reachable), and no openable source I found (OpenStax Biology 2e, Concepts of Biology, Microbiology) describes the fluctuation test. Not verified on trust. Per the brief: if it cannot be checked, cut this reveal sentence; the lesson stands on c1-c3. Needs a web-capable session (W-583) or an openable copy. | FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Learner text (Demo.tsx line 189): 'Luria and Delbrück found jackpots like these in 1943, with a virus instead of a drug: evidence that resistance mutations arise at random before the threat, not in answer to it.' Opened on PMC: the paper's record, Luria and Delbrück (1943), 'Mutations of Bacteria from Virus Sensitivity to Virus Resistance', Genetics 28(6): 491-511, doi 10.1093/genetics/28.6.491 (PMC1209226; citation and authors confirmed; the body is a scanned PDF I did not read). Also Meneely, 'Pick Your Poisson: An Educational Primer for Luria and Delbrück's Classic Paper', Genetics 2016, 202(2): 371-375 (PMC4766000). It describes the 'mutation to immunity' hypothesis, which 'predicts that resistant bacteria were present in the population before infection by the phages'. In one experiment '11 of the 20 cultures had no resistant colonies ... three cultures had many more resistant colonies, from 35 to 107. These are Luria's jackpots.' The data 'constitute strong evidence that mutations arise at random without regard to their selective advantage'. Phage = a virus that infects bacteria (the primer: 'bacteriophages (i.e., viruses that infect bacteria)'). All parts hold.

claims.text: 20 identical cultures each grow from one cell to about a million (20 doublings); resistance mutations strike at random during divisions, about once per million. Under 'made by the drug' there are no mutations during growth and each cell on the plate turns resistant with chance 10 in 2^20.
claims.source: Toy choices from the brief (rates, 20 generations, every non-mutant cell dies on the plate), stated on the stage.
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Convention, stated on the locked stage ('20 identical cultures each grow from one cell to about a million. Resistance mutations strike at random during divisions, about once per million'); code: GENS 20 (2^20 = 1,048,576), per-division rate non/2^20, drug rule Poisson(10) = 2^20 x 10/2^20. The rates are toy choices; no real mutation rate is claimed.

recall.question: Ten identical yeast cultures are tested for a rare resistance. Nine have no resistant cells and one has hundreds. Which idea does this fit better?
options: Mutations arose at random during growth, before the test
The test itself made some cells resistant
Neither: the cultures cannot have been identical
recall.why: Random mutations during growth give jackpots: an early mutant is copied into many descendants in one culture. Resistance caused by the test would give similar counts in every culture.
